prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a coarse room layout: the TV and media console remain roughly 2–3 m in front of the camera wearer, the shelving units flank them at similar depth, and the bed or sofa occupies the right foreground, ranging from about 0.3–1.5 m away. In frames 1–2, the foreground furniture on the right is much nearer than the TV, while the left floor cushion is roughly 1–2 m away; in frame 3, camera rotation and motion blur make these boundaries uncertain. By frames 4–5, the camera is closer to or above the bed, with bedding, a hand, and the dark animal-shaped foreground region within arm’s reach, while the TV remains several metres ahead and above the bed surface. The map makes near-versus-far layering and partial occlusion by bedding clearer than RGB alone, but it appears unreliable on the bright TV screen, fine shelf structure, object edges, and the partly out-of-view foreground forms.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map separates the TV near the upper centre-left from the bed or sofa entering from the lower right, showing that the bed increasingly occludes the floor and lower furniture as the camera turns right from frames 1–3 and settles facing the TV in frames 4–5. It repeatedly labels the on-screen figure as a person, but this is a person depicted on the TV about 2–3 m away rather than someone physically occupying the room; the detected region faces outward toward the camera because of the screen image. In later frames, cyan regions labelled person appear along the lower edge where RGB instead shows a close dark animal-shaped form, bedding, or body parts, so those detections are spatially unreliable and partly outside the frame. The map clarifies object extents and occlusion order better than RGB, but omits most shelves, small objects, cushions, and the camera wearer’s visible hand, and its masks do not provide dependable metric distances.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is entirely black across all five frames, so it supplies no body or hand landmarks, orientations, gaze directions, reach estimates, or changes in human pose. In the RGB frames, the only clearly visible human figure is displayed on the TV rather than physically present in the room, while a camera-wearer hand appears near the bottom edge in the later frames and is within immediate reach of the bedding. Because neither that close hand nor the televised figure produces a skeleton, the map cannot resolve facing direction, joint position, occlusion, or whether any person looks toward the camera wearer. Its absence is itself evidence that pose detection failed or found no eligible physical person, making this map unreliable for spatial analysis here.
